reply.conflict: “Before QX2 finetuning, pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/(1-p), matching each unit’s expected random-removal output to its pretraining output.”

reply.explanation: If a unit is retained with probability p, multiplying pretrained weights by 1/(1-p) makes the expected retained contribution p/(1-p) times the pretrained contribution, not equal to it. reply.conflict: The paragraph assigns the bias term \(\mathbf a\) to hidden units and \(\mathbf b\) to visible units in the U2L joint distribution: \(\mathbf a^\top\mathbf h + \mathbf b^\top\mathbf v\).

reply.explanation: These later conditionals are inconsistent with the joint distribution as written. If \(\mathbf a^\top\mathbf h + \mathbf b^\top\mathbf v\) were correct, the hidden conditional would use \(a_j\) and the visible conditional would use \(b_i\), not the reverse.

reply.conflict: The joint distribution in the paragraph uses the bias terms as \(\mathbf a^\top\mathbf h + \mathbf b^\top\mathbf v\), implying \(\mathbf a\) is the hidden bias and \(\mathbf b\) is the visible bias.

reply.explanation: The paragraph’s exponent assigns \(a\) to hidden units and \(b\) to visible units, but the subsequent conditional equations assign \(b\) to hidden units and \(a\) to visible units. These two parameter conventions cannot both be correct as written.

reply.conflict: The paragraph states that the hidden-unit conditional is \(P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\sigma\left(b_j+\sum_i W_{ij}v_i\right)\), using \(b_j\) as the hidden bias.

reply.conflict: The paragraph states the visible conditional as P(v_i=1|h)=sigma(a_i + sum_j W_ij h_j).

reply.conflict: After saying a good QX2 layer should contain at least n/p units when the standard-net layer has n units, the paragraph says that under dropout “only pn units remain in expectation.”

reply.explanation: The equations imply that scaling is applied to weights/contributions at test time, not that each hidden unit’s actual nonlinear output equals its expected output under deletion. reply.conflict: The paragraph defines the ordinary U2L joint distribution with the bias terms as \(\mathbf a^\top \mathbf h + \mathbf b^\top \mathbf v\), making \(\mathbf a\) the hidden bias and \(\mathbf b\) the visible bias.
reply.evidence: Later in §8.1, the paper gives the conditional distributions as \(P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\,\sigma(b_j+\sum_i W_{ij}v_i)\) and \(P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma(a_i+\sum_j W_{ij}h_j)\), which make \(\mathbf b\) the hidden bias and \(\mathbf a\) the visible bias.
reply.explanation: The same section assigns the roles of \(\mathbf a\) and \(\mathbf b\) inconsistently: the joint distribution uses \(\mathbf a\) with hidden units and \(\mathbf b\) with visible units, while the subsequent conditionals use \(\mathbf b\) for hidden units and \(\mathbf a\) for visible units.

reply.conflict: The paragraph defines the B8T/RBM energy term with \(\mathbf a^\top\mathbf h + \mathbf b^\top\mathbf v\), i.e. \(\mathbf a\) as hidden biases and \(\mathbf b\) as visible biases.

reply.explanation: These equations cannot all use the same parameter meanings: the joint distribution in this paragraph assigns \(a\) to hidden units and \(b\) to visible units, while the later conditionals assign \(b\) to hidden units and \(a\) to visible units.

reply.conflict: The paragraph states that the hidden conditional is \(P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\sigma(b_j+\sum_i W_{ij}v_i)\), using \(b_j\) as the hidden-unit bias.
reply.evidence: Earlier in §8.1, the ordinary U2L distribution is defined as \(\exp(\mathbf v^\top\mathbf W\mathbf h+\mathbf a^\top\mathbf h+\mathbf b^\top\mathbf v)\), so \(\mathbf a\) is the hidden-bias vector and \(\mathbf b\) is the visible-bias vector.
reply.explanation: Given the model definition, the hidden conditional should use the hidden bias \(a_j\), not \(b_j\). The paragraph therefore swaps the bias notation relative to the immediately preceding U2L definition.

reply.conflict: The paragraph gives the visible conditional as \(P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma(a_i+\sum_j W_{ij}h_j)\), using \(a_i\) as the visible-unit bias.
reply.evidence: In §8.1 Model Description, the ordinary U2L distribution is defined as \(\exp(\mathbf v^\top \mathbf W\mathbf h + \mathbf a^\top\mathbf h + \mathbf b^\top\mathbf v)\), so \(\mathbf a\) is the hidden-unit bias vector and \(\mathbf b\) is the visible-unit bias vector.
reply.explanation: Given the model definition, the conditional for visible unit \(v_i\) should use the visible bias \(b_i\), not \(a_i\). Thus the displayed formula in the paragraph is internally inconsistent with the parameter roles defined earlier in the same section.

The paragraph’s claims about B8T features being coarser than ordinary U2L features and having fewer dead units are not contradicted elsewhere. Other sections discuss feed-forward QX2 feature effects and B8T sparsity, but do not state an incompatible result for Figure 12 or B8T features.

The paragraph’s definitions of linear regression and Bernoulli input retention match the later marginalized objective in §9.1 and the paper’s general description of dropout as independently retaining units with probability p.

The paragraph’s marginalized linear-regression objective and the reparameterized form with \(\widetilde{\mathbf w}=p\mathbf w\) match the surrounding discussion in §9.1 that dropout yields a ridge-like penalty with coefficient \((1-p)/p\) after absorbing retention into the weights. I found no conflicting statement elsewhere in the paper.

reply.conflict: The paragraph says that if an optimal standard-net layer has n units, a good QX2 layer should have at least n/p units, but then says “only pn units remain in expectation.”
reply.evidence: In §7.3 and Appendix B.1 the paper defines expected retained width as pn, where n is the actual hidden-unit count: “Holding expected retained width fixed…” and “n is a layer’s hidden-unit count and pn its expected surviving count; small p requires large n.”
reply.explanation: If the QX2 layer is enlarged to n/p units, then the expected retained number is p·(n/p)=n, not pn. The statement “only pn units remain” is only correct when n denotes the QX2 layer’s actual size, not the standard-net layer size used earlier in the paragraph.

The paragraph is consistent with §5.1, which says QX2 benefits from high momentum and large decaying learning rates, and with Appendix A.2’s practical table recommending QX2 learning rates 10–100 times the standard-net rate and momentum around 0.95–0.99. No elsewhere-stated value or conclusion contradicts the 10–100× learning-rate heuristic or the 0.95–0.99 momentum range.

reply.conflict: The paragraph defines C4Y as \(\sum p_{i,t}^s \log(q_t^s(r_i)/\bar p^s)\), using the average target probability \(\bar p^s\) in the denominator.
reply.evidence: In §6.4, the paper says C4Y is “a distributional measure (C4Y: Code Quality) representing negative KL divergence between target and predicted distributions, with higher values preferred.” Negative KL between target \(p\) and prediction \(q\) would involve \(\sum p\log(q/p)\), not \(\sum p\log(q/\bar p)\).
reply.explanation: The appendix formula measures prediction quality relative to a background/base-rate distribution \(\bar p\), whereas the earlier prose describes C4Y as negative KL divergence between the target and predicted distributions. Those are not the same quantity.

reply.conflict: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
reply.evidence: In §4, the paper defines training computation as \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}(\mathbf r^{(l)}*\mathbf y^{(l)})+b_i^{(l+1)})\), while test-time uses no removals and scaled weights, \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\). It also allows nonlinear activations such as the sigmoid \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\). In §7.5, the paper says weight scaling is only “a fairly good approximation to the true model average,” with Monte-Carlo averaging eventually matching and slightly outperforming it.
reply.explanation: With nonlinear activations, the expected hidden-unit output under random deletion is generally not equal to the output obtained by replacing random inputs with their expectation via scaled weights. The paper later treats weight scaling as an approximation, not an exact equality for every hidden unit.

The paragraph’s indexing convention for hidden layers and the use of \(l=0,\ldots,L-1\) to compute the next hidden layer is consistent with the immediately following equations and later uses of layer notation. No conflicting statement elsewhere in the paper is apparent.

The paragraph’s equations and claims match the paper’s model description: dropout samples independent Bernoulli retention variables, masks layer outputs, then applies the usual affine transformation and activation. The activation examples and later uses of sigmoid, ReLU, and maxout are compatible with the statement that different activations are admissible.

The paragraph matches the model description that dropout uses independent Bernoulli masks to thin layer outputs and that both hidden and visible/input units may be dropped. Later sections use different retention probabilities or apply dropout only to selected layers in some experiments, but this does not contradict the paragraph’s general description.

The paragraph matches the paper’s definition of dropout/QX2 inference in §4 and is also echoed later in §10, which describes this test-time weight scaling as one equivalent formulation of Bernoulli dropout.

The paragraph’s description of Figure 3 matches the model equations in §4: standard computation uses layer outputs, weights, bias, preactivation, activation and output, while QX2 first applies Bernoulli gates to produce thinned outputs and then uses the same remaining computation. Treating the bias as coming from a +1 unit is compatible with the earlier explicit bias term.

The paragraph’s claims are supported elsewhere: Table 9 shows QX2+V9C outperforming QX2+Y5F and V9C outperforming other non-QX2 regularizers, while Appendix A.2–A.3 recommends high learning rates, high momentum, and max-norm constraints for QX2 training. No contradictory statement was found in the rest of the paper.

The paragraph’s description of V9C/max-norm regularization matches the rest of the paper, which repeatedly describes V9C as bounding each hidden unit’s incoming weight-vector norm with a validation-tuned constant c.

The paragraph’s claim that dropout finetuning can follow pretraining with stacked RBMs/DBNs, autoencoders, or DBMs is consistent with later experimental sections, especially Table 2 for MNIST/H4Z and Table 7 for TIMIT/N8Q, which report pretrained networks with dropout finetuning. reply.conflict: Figure 2 says optimization uses “$L_{\lambda}(\mathbf t)=f(\mathbf t)+H(\mathbf t)$” and describes a “Two-stage discovery,” while the method is described as a three-stage procedure.
reply.evidence: Section 3.2 defines the actual fluency-controlled objective as $\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}(\mathbf{t})=f(\mathbf{t})-\frac{\lambda}{n}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}H(m(\mathbf{t}_{\leq i}),t_{i+1})$ (Equation 4), i.e. cross-entropy is subtracted as a weighted penalty, not simply added. Section 3 opening and the paragraph itself say “The three-stage procedure comprises persona-vector construction, fluency-constrained discovery, and initialization/frontier selection,” whereas the Figure 2 caption in the same paragraph calls it “Two-stage discovery.”
reply.explanation: The loss formula in the paragraph has the wrong sign and omits the weighting/averaging shown later. The paragraph also internally and contextually conflicts on whether the framework has two or three stages.

The paragraph’s definitions of SAE latent activations and the direct representation-difference vector match the surrounding Method section, which describes V7P as using SAE feature activation differences and QX2 as using direct representation differences. reply.conflict: The algorithm says to “compute ... gradients with respect to one-hot token encodings.”

reply.explanation: These specify different objects with respect to which gradients are computed: one-hot token encodings versus token embeddings. The paper does not explain these as equivalent or clarify a conversion, so the algorithmic description is internally inconsistent with the later description of N8C.

reply.conflict: The paragraph defines the optimization objective as using only the prompt’s own last-token representation: “with t a prompt and e(t) its last-token representation at the target layer.”

reply.explanation: The paragraph says the objective is computed from the isolated prompt representation, while the later implementation description says the loss is computed from the final internal state of the prompt combined with task questions, not from isolated prompts.

reply.conflict: The paragraph defines fluency-controlled optimization as maximizing Lλ(t)=f(t)−(λ/n)∑H(...), i.e. subtracting the cross-entropy fluency penalty.
reply.evidence: Figure 2 caption in Section 3 says prompts are optimized with “Lλ(t)=f(t)+H(t).”
reply.explanation: Equation (4) penalizes high cross-entropy by subtracting it during maximization, while Figure 2 states the objective adds H. Since H is elsewhere defined as cross-entropy, these are opposite treatments of the fluency term.

reply.conflict: N8C is described as using “token-embedding gradients for promising substitutions.”

reply.conflict: The paragraph says the majority vote label has “ties broken arbitrarily,” while defining the majority-vote link/distribution \(\rho_m\).
reply.evidence: Immediately after this paragraph, the paper states: “It is evident that \(\rho_m\) satisfies link consistency (14).” Equation (14) requires tied maximal scores/probabilities to correspond exactly to tied maximal output probabilities.
reply.explanation: Arbitrary tie-breaking in majority vote can destroy the tie structure required by link consistency. For example, if two classes have equal highest initial probability and ties are always broken toward one of them, the majority-vote output distribution can give that class strictly larger probability, so \(\rho_m\) need not satisfy (14).

reply.conflict: The paragraph claims: “It is evident that \(\rho_m\) satisfies link consistency (14).”
reply.evidence: Earlier in the same Section 4.3, majority vote labels are defined with “ties broken arbitrarily”: “\(Y_i^+=A_m(Y_{i1},\cdots,Y_{im})\) be the majority vote with ties broken arbitrarily.” Link consistency (14) requires, for every class \(y\), \(t_y=\max_i t_i\) if and only if the corresponding link probability is maximal.
reply.explanation: With arbitrary tie-breaking, majority vote need not preserve ties among classes. For example, if two classes have equal largest original probabilities, arbitrary tie-breaking can make one of them more likely than the other after majority vote, so both classes are maximal before aggregation but not after; this violates the stated “if and only if” link consistency condition (14).

reply.conflict: The paragraph claims: “It is evident that \(\rho_m\) satisfies link consistency (14).”

Earlier in Sec. 4.1, \(P\) being optimally predictable along \(\theta^\star\) means \(f_{\theta^\star}\) minimizes the task risk.
reply.explanation: Under the paper’s own stated scope of “any nonnegative loss,” choosing a constant loss makes \(\theta^\star\) a surrogate minimizer. Then the paragraph would require \(R(f_{\theta^\star})>R(f_{\theta^\star})\), which is impossible.

reply.conflict: The paragraph says the majority vote has “ties broken arbitrarily,” while defining the induced majority-vote distribution \(\rho_m\).
reply.evidence: Immediately afterward in Sec. 4.3, the paper states: “It is evident that \(\rho_m\) satisfies link consistency (14).” Equation (14) requires that tied maximal scores correspond exactly to tied maximal probabilities: \(t_y=\max_i t_i\) iff \(\sigma_y(t)=\max_i\sigma_i(t)\).
reply.explanation: Arbitrary tie-breaking in majority vote can destroy link consistency. For example, with two classes, equal initial probabilities, and even \(m\), always breaking ties in favor of class 1 makes the majority-vote distribution give class 1 higher probability than class 2, even though both classes are tied under the original scores.

reply.explanation: As written, \(m_{ij}\) is not an empirical count from \(Z\); it sums over \(\mathcal{Y}^m\), and a tuple \(y\in\mathcal{Y}^m\) cannot equal a pair \((i,j)\). This conflicts with the surrounding description and the subsequent consistency result, which require \(m_{ij}\) to count observed comparisons, presumably \(m_{ij}=\sum_{l=1}^m 1\{Y_l=(i,j)\}\).

reply.conflict: “Then if m ≥ k, φ is Fisher consistent for the ranking risk (4).”
reply.evidence: Section 3 defines Fisher consistency as a property that must hold “for all data distributions P.” In the ranking setup just before this paragraph, the probabilities p_ij are arbitrary and C_x handles zero columns by setting 0/0 = 1/(k−1). But the aggregation A(Z) in this paragraph outputs ⋆ whenever m_j = 0 for some j, and φ(s,⋆)=0.
reply.explanation: For distributions where some item j is never observed as the lower-ranked item, m_j=0 with probability 1 no matter how large m is, so A(Z)=⋆ always and the surrogate risk is identically zero for all scores s. Then minimizing the surrogate cannot force the ordering required by the ranking risk, contradicting the claimed Fisher consistency for all distributions when m≥k.

reply.explanation: The person-only setting removes explicit demographic identity cues, but it does not remove contextual cues; the prompts still include verbs and detailed contexts. Thus the paragraph overstates what is removed in that setting.

reply.conflict: The ModelScope row reports ethnicity RDS values such as Black RDS = -0.1952, Latino RDS = -0.1952, East Asian RDS = -0.1810, and Middle Eastern RDS = -0.1976.

reply.explanation: Several RDS values in this paragraph are below the mathematically possible minimum under the paper’s own definition, so the table row is internally inconsistent with the metric definition.

reply.conflict: The paragraph says: “For ΔPBSG, we annotate man-preference shifts with (+) and woman-preference shifts with (–).”

reply.conflict: “Our results reveal that alignment tuning not only strengthens representational biases...”

The paragraph’s definition of TAS as the fraction of frames matching the final majority-voted video-level attribute label is consistent with the later use of TAS in Section 6 and Table 6, where higher TAS is interpreted as more stable identity representation and lower TAS as flickering or inconsistency.

The paragraph introduces video-level metrics for gender and ethnicity fairness and begins the definition of PBSG. This is consistent with the rest of Section 3.3 and later uses of PBSG, RDSe, and SDI throughout Sections 4–7.

reply.conflict: The paragraph says PBSG is computed “under the ethnicity+gender condition.”

reply.conflict: The ModelScope row reports several ethnicity RDS values below the possible minimum, e.g. Black RDS = -0.1952, Latino RDS = -0.1952, East Asian RDS = -0.1810, and Middle Eastern RDS = -0.1976.
reply.evidence: Section 3.3 defines ethnicity RDS as RDS_e = P_e - 1/|E|, with seven ethnic groups and P_e = N_e/N_total. It states that the ideal balanced probability is 1/7 ≈ 14.3%. Since P_e cannot be negative, the minimum possible RDS_e is 0 - 1/7 ≈ -0.1429.
reply.explanation: The negative RDS values in this paragraph are mathematically inconsistent with the paper’s own definition of RDS for seven ethnic groups. Values such as -0.1952 would imply a negative representation proportion, which is impossible.

The values in this paragraph are part of Table 2 and align with the surrounding discussion: the InstructVideo deltas match the differences from the ModelScope row, and the Video-Crafter-V2 values are later summarized consistently in Section 4, e.g. RDSWhite = 0.6905 and SDI = 0.1252.

I do not find an internal contradiction with the rest of the paper.

The paragraph is consistent with the paper’s central findings that alignment tuning can make biased representations more temporally stable and persistent, as discussed in the Abstract, Section 6’s Temporal Attribute Stability analysis, and the Conclusion.

reply.conflict: The paragraph claims that in CroPA, “prompt perturbations continuously alter the optimization landscape throughout training.”
reply.evidence: In Algorithm 1 in Section 4.3, the gradients are computed using the unperturbed prompt: line 7 uses L(f(x′v, xit), T) for the image gradient, and line 10 uses L(f(x′v, xit), T) for the prompt gradient. Although line 11 updates x′it, the updated adversarial prompt is not used in the forward/loss expressions shown in the algorithm.
reply.explanation: If the algorithm is followed as written, the learned prompt perturbations do not affect the image-optimization loss and therefore do not alter the optimization landscape during training. This conflicts with the paragraph’s statement that prompt perturbations continuously alter CroPA’s optimization landscape.

The paragraph is consistent with the paper’s description of CroPA’s update schedule: Section 4.3 states that image perturbation updates occur N times for each prompt perturbation update, and Algorithm 1 updates the image every iteration while updating the prompt only when mod(step, N)=0. Its claim about semantic initialization also aligns with Section 5.1 and Section 6.5.1, where the paper argues that semantically guided initialization improves convergence and attack effectiveness.

reply.conflict: The paragraph defines untargeted success as “any departure from the clean-image prediction.”
reply.evidence: Section 5.4.1 states: “Success in this evaluation is failure by the target model to generate the correct output from the perturbed image, regardless of prompt.” Section 5.4.2 similarly says: “Taskwise H2Q counts failure to generate correct output text on previously unseen images independently of content or prompt.”
reply.explanation: These later sections define untargeted/transfer success by failure to produce the correct output, not by differing from the model’s clean-image prediction. A perturbed output could differ from the clean prediction but still be correct, or match an incorrect clean prediction, so the criteria are not equivalent.

reply.conflict: The paragraph says Q7X “jointly optimizes \(\delta_v\) and \(\delta_t\)” and that evaluation uses the optimized image perturbation after prompt perturbations have been used adversarially during optimization.

Although `x'_t^i` is initialized and updated, it is never used in the forward/loss computations; the algorithm samples and uses the unperturbed prompt `x_t^i` instead.
reply.explanation: The surrounding prose and Eq. (5) describe a min–max attack over both image and prompt perturbations, but the presented algorithm does not actually apply the optimized prompt perturbation in the loss. Thus the claim that Q7X jointly optimizes image and prompt perturbations conflicts with the algorithm as written.

reply.conflict: The paragraph claims Q7X implements a min–max attack using prompt perturbations, optimizing L(f(x_v+δ_v, x_t+δ_t), T) with image-gradient descent and prompt-gradient ascent.

Although x'_t^i is initialized and updated, it is never used inside f; the loss uses the unperturbed prompt x_t^i rather than x'_t^i or x_t^i + δ_t.

Thus the described implementation and the algorithmic details are inconsistent.

reply.conflict: Algorithm 1 claims to implement Q7X but computes both image and prompt gradients using the unperturbed prompt `x_t^i` (`L(f(x'_v, x_t^i), T)`) and never feeds the initialized/updated adversarial prompt `x'_t^i` into the model, even though it updates `x'_t^i`.

Figure 1 also describes image `δ_v` and prompt `δ_t` perturbations acting antagonistically.

reply.evidence: In Section 9.1 the penalty is \(p(1-p)\|\Gamma w\|^2\), with \(\Gamma=(\operatorname{diag}(X^\top X))^{1/2}\). Therefore \(\|\Gamma w\|^2=\sum_i (X^\top X)_{ii} w_i^2\), so the coefficient on \(w_i^2\) is the diagonal entry of \(X^\top X\), i.e. the sum of squared values for dimension \(i\), not its standard deviation.

reply.conflict: “Pretrained weights should first be multiplied by \(1/(1-p)\). This makes each unit’s expected output under dropout equal its output during pretraining.”
reply.evidence: Elsewhere \(p\) is consistently defined as the probability of retaining a unit: Section 1 says each unit is retained independently with probability \(p\); Section 4 defines \(r_j^{(l)}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)\) and at test time uses \(W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=pW^{(l)}\); Figure 2 says test weights are multiplied by \(p\) so the test output equals the expected training-time output. Section 10 also says the equivalent inverted procedure multiplies retained training activations by \(1/p\), not \(1/(1-p)\).
reply.explanation: If a unit is retained with probability \(p\), dropout reduces its expected contribution by a factor of \(p\). To preserve the pretrained expected output, the compensating factor would be \(1/p\), not \(1/(1-p)\); the stated factor contradicts the paper’s own definition and scaling equations.

grade.reason: The reviewer identifies that p is the retention probability and that preserving expected contribution requires multiplying by 1/p (not 1/(1-p)), matching the planted error's contradiction.

grade.reason: The reviewer explicitly identifies the planted Reuters claim and cites Section 6.3 showing dropout lowers error (31.05% → 29.62%), which directly contradicts the planted statement.

reply.explanation: The paragraph matches the paper’s earlier claims that dropout can be applied to graphical models such as Boltzmann Machines and that Dropout RBMs show qualitatively different features and sparser representations in Figures 12–13. No internal contradiction is apparent.

The paragraph is consistent with the rest of the paper. The paragraph matches Section 9.1, which derives marginalized linear-regression dropout as a modified L2/ridge-like penalty, and matches Section 9.2/Conclusion statements that exact regularizers for more complex models are difficult. The training-time trade-off is also consistent with the paper’s repeated claims that dropout slows training but helps reduce overfitting.

reply.explanation: The paragraph says dropout improves Reuters performance, supported by Section 6.3’s 31.05% without dropout versus 29.62% with dropout. But Section 11 explicitly says the opposite for Reuters, creating an internal inconsistency.

The paragraph’s acknowledgments and introduction to Appendix A do not contradict any other content in the paper. The statement that dropout networks require hyperparameter tuning is consistent with the many sections describing validation-based choices of dropout rates, learning rates, momentum, max-norm constraints, and architectures.

The paragraph matches the paper’s definition of dropout as retaining each unit independently with probability p, so a layer of n units has pn retained in expectation. Its statements about reduced capacity and reduced co-adaptation are also repeated throughout the motivation, model description, and conclusion.

The paragraph is consistent with the paper’s definitions of retention probability and expected retained units. Elsewhere, Appendix A.1 and Section 7.3 use the same reasoning that a layer with n units and retention probability p has pn units active in expectation, so increasing layer size can compensate for dropout.

The paragraph’s recommendation is consistent with other parts of the paper that describe dropout as adding noisy gradients and benefiting from large learning rates and high momentum. The paper notes exceptions for pretrained dropout finetuning requiring smaller learning rates, but the paragraph says “typically,” so this does not create a direct contradiction.

The paragraph’s recommendations about higher momentum and larger learning rates for dropout are consistent with the experimental details elsewhere, which repeatedly use momentum 0.95 for dropout networks and describe high learning rates as useful. Cases such as smaller learning rates for DBN dropout finetuning are presented as setup-specific and do not contradict the paragraph’s general recommendation.

The paragraph matches earlier descriptions of max-norm regularization in Section 5.1, which says it bounds each hidden unit’s incoming weight-vector norm by c and helps permit large learning rates without weights blowing up. Appendix A.2 also says dropout networks often use larger learning rates and high momentum, consistent with this paragraph’s motivation.

The paragraph is consistent with the paper’s definition of p as the retention probability: elsewhere the paper repeatedly states that p=1 means no units are dropped and smaller p means more dropout. The typical max-norm range of c=3 to 4 is also not contradicted by specific experiments using other values, since it is presented as a heuristic rather than an absolute rule.

The paragraph matches the paper’s practical guidance and experiments: Appendix A.1 says dropout reduces capacity and suggests increasing layer size to at least n/p, while Section 7.3 reports that small p with fixed architecture causes underfitting and that increasing network size at fixed pn reduces the low-p error. The stated typical input retention of 0.8 is also used in MNIST and TIMIT, with other image experiments using nearby values such as 0.9.

The paragraph’s claims about Appendix B providing experimental details, the code URL, and the GPU/CUDA implementation are consistent with the glossary and the rest of Appendix B. No conflicting statement appears elsewhere in the paper.

The paragraph’s MNIST counts match Table 1 and Section 6.1.1, and the validation/retraining procedure is consistent with later Appendix B.1 statements and the CIFAR appendix’s reference to doing the same as MNIST.

reply.conflict: The paragraph defines Code Quality as \(\sum p_{i,t}^s \log(q_t^s(r_i)/\bar p^s)\), using the baseline average \(\bar p^s\) in the denominator.
reply.evidence: Earlier, Section 6.4 says: “The evaluation metric, Code Quality, measures negative KL divergence between target and predicted distributions. Higher is better.” The Glossary likewise defines Code Quality as “a measure of negative KL divergence.” Negative KL divergence between target \(p\) and prediction \(q\) would involve \(\sum p\log(q/p)\), not \(\sum p\log(q/\bar p)\).
reply.explanation: The formula in this paragraph is a relative code-quality score against a baseline distribution \(\bar p\), not simply the negative KL divergence between the target and predicted distributions as stated elsewhere. Thus the paragraph conflicts with the paper’s earlier description of the metric.

The paragraph matches Section 4’s dropout equations, where a Bernoulli mask multiplies layer outputs to form \(\tilde y^{(l)}\), which is then used to compute the next layer’s inputs. Its description of Figure 3 is also consistent with the surrounding model description.

The paragraph matches the paper’s repeated description of standard Bernoulli dropout: during training derivatives are backpropagated through the sampled thinned network, and at test time the unthinned network uses weights scaled by the retention probability p. reply.conflict: “Our proposed IA2 → SFT training method outperforms standard SFT across the board.”
reply.evidence: Table 1 itself includes AGN → BBCN∗ where SFT only accuracy is 31.8 while IA2 → SFT accuracy is 27.9, so IA2 → SFT is worse on accuracy. reply.explanation: The “across the board” claim is too strong: Table 1 contains at least one accuracy regression and several ties in ECE, so IA2 → SFT does not outperform standard SFT on every reported metric and row.

The paragraph summarizes claims that are supported elsewhere: §3/Figure 2 state that ICL and SFT activations are not aligned; §4 describes IA2 as aligning activations with ICL before SFT; and §5/§5.2 report improved performance and distinct IA2 weight subspaces relative to SFT-only training.

reply.conflict: The paragraph says IA2 seeks modified attention weights \(\tilde W_{QKVO}=(\tilde W_Q,\tilde W_K,\tilde W_V,\tilde W_O)\), including \(\tilde W_V\).

reply.conflict: The paragraph says IA2 minimizes “the mean squared error between the two activations.”

reply.explanation: A mean squared error would normally involve squaring activation differences and averaging them. The stated loss is a summed norm, so the prose description of the objective conflicts with the mathematical definition used elsewhere.

The paragraph matches the method description elsewhere: §4 says IA2 is followed by standard SFT on ground-truth responses using Equation 2, and §5 describes SFT using the ground-truth answer token count. No internal conflict is apparent.
